rows.label: Study notes
rows.text: **Specific Heat Capacity:** This topic covers the fundamental concepts of specific heat capacity in the physics curriculum.  ·  Understanding specific heat capacity is essential for solving problems and building higher-level mathematical skills.  ·  Key definitions and theorems related to specific heat capacity should be memorized and practiced regularly.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: Concept 5: Connection between Specific Heat Capacity and other topics  ·  Key Formula 5: Important relation in Specific Heat Capacity  ·  ❌ Specific heat depends on the shape/size of the object. ✅ Specific heat is an INTENSIVE property - it depends only on the material, not on the object's shape, size, or mass. A gold ring and a gold bar have the same $c$.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ❌ $c_p$ and $c_v$ are the same for all substances. ✅ For solids and liquids, $c_p \approx c_v$ because they barely expand. For gases, $c_p > c_v$ significantly because gases expand and do work. The difference is $c_p - c_v = R/M$ (per kg) or $R$ (per mole).  ·  ❌ A substance with high specific heat is always "hotter." ✅ High $c$ means the substance RESISTS temperature change - it takes a lot of heat to raise its temperature. Water at 20°C has high $c$ but isn't "hot" - it just requires a lot of energy to change its temperature.  ·  ❌ The specific heat of water is 1 cal/g·°C everywhere. ✅ The calorie is DEFINED using water's specific heat, but that specific heat varies slightly with temperature. At 15°C, $c = 4.1855\text{ J/g·K}$ (giving 1 cal = 4.1855 J). The modern exact value is $1\text{ cal} = 4.184\text{ J}$ (thermochemical calorie).

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ❌ Gases have only one specific heat capacity. ✅ Gases have TWO: $c_p$ (constant pressure) and $c_v$ (constant volume). $c_p - c_v = R$ per mole, or $c_p - c_v = R/M$ per unit mass. For air, $c_p = 1005$ and $c_v = 718\text{ J/kg·K}$.  ·  ❌ Metals always have low specific heat. ✅ While most metals do have low $c$ (because they're dense and atoms are heavy), beryllium ($c = 1825$) and lithium ($c = 3580$) are exceptions - they have low atomic mass, so per kg they have many atoms and high heat capacity.  ·  ❌ $c$ has dimensions of $[ML^2T^{-2}]$. ✅ $c = H/(m\Delta\theta)$, so $[c] = [ML^2T^{-2}] / ([M][\Theta]) = [L^2T^{-2}\Theta^{-1}]$. Mass dimension CANCELS. The $[M^0]$ is the key difference from heat capacity.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ❌ J/kg·K and J/kg·°C are different units. ✅ Since these units involve a TEMPERATURE INTERVAL (Δθ), and 1 K = 1°C in size, J/kg·K and J/kg·°C are EXACTLY the same. Only absolute temperatures differ.  ·  ❌ The dimensional formula depends on the system of units. ✅ Dimensional formulas are system-independent. Whether you use SI or CGS, $[c] = [L^2T^{-2}\Theta^{-1}]$. Only the numerical VALUES change, not the dimensions.  ·  ❌ Heat capacity has the same dimensions as specific heat. ✅ Heat capacity $C = mc$ has $[C] = [ML^2T^{-2}\Theta^{-1}]$ - it includes the mass dimension $[M]$ because it depends on the amount of substance.

rows.label: More ideas
rows.text: ❌ $c$ can have negative dimensions. ✅ Specific heat is always positive for normal materials. Negative $c$ would mean adding heat lowers temperature, which violates thermodynamics (except in exotic gravitational systems like stars).  ·  ❌ $1\text{ cal/g·°C} = 1\text{ J/kg·K}$. ✅ They differ by a factor of 4184. The calorie is about 4184 times larger than the joule, and the gram is 1/1000 of a kilogram, so the ratio is $4184 \times 1000 / 1000 = 4184$.  ·  Note 3: Practice numerical problems regularly for mastery of Specific Heat Capacity
